papers.title: Issues arising from medical system's failure
papers.abstract: As more health-care providers adopt and utilise information technology in the treatment of there patients, so the number of system failures increases. Analysis of these failures shows us that these systems are failing for a variety of technical and social reason. The question that we are forced to ask is Why? In this paper I seek to highlight some of the problems that are currently facing developers and users of medical computing systems.

variable_details.name: Perivascular Elastic Modulus Gradient (PEMG)
variable_details.description: A spatially varying effective elastic modulus of the perivascular ECM that determines how much the astrocytic endfeet can deform during each cardiac cycle. PEMG is hypothesized to decline with age due to collagen cross‑linking and loss of hyaluronic acid, creating a stiffening gradient that attenuates the astrocytic pump.
variable_details.mathematical_formulation:
PEMG(r) = E_0 * exp( - r / λ_E ) * (1 + α_age ),
where r is radial distance from the arterial wall, E_0 is baseline modulus at birth, λ_E is decay length of ECM compliance, and α_age ≥ 0 captures age‑dependent stiffening (α_age = k_s * (Age – Age_0)).
variable_details.derivation: Starting from the linear elastic relation σ = E·ε for the perivascular sheath, the pressure‑driven deformation of astrocytic endfeet (Δr) during systole is Δr = ΔP·r / PEMG(r). The convective velocity component v_conv ∝ Δr·f_heart, giving v_conv(r) = f_heart·ΔP·r / PEMG(r). Substituting PEMG(r) yields a closed‑form expression linking ECM stiffness to flow speed.

predictions.description: In young mice (Age < 3 months) the measured perivascular CSF velocity (v) will follow v(r) ≈ C·r·exp( - r / λ_E ), whereas in aged mice (Age > 18 months) the same profile will be reduced by a factor ≈ 1/(1+α_age).
predictions.expected_magnitude: For typical ΔP = 5 mmHg, f_heart = 10 Hz, E_0 = 0.5 kPa, λ_E = 150 µm, α_age ≈ 1.5 in old mice, predicted peak velocity drops from ~30 µm/s to ~12 µm/s.

predictions.description: Pharmacological softening of the ECM (e.g., hyaluronidase injection) will restore v_conv to ~80 % of young‑mouse values even in old mice, without altering AQP4 expression.
predictions.expected_magnitude: A 30 % reduction in PEMG should increase v_conv by ~30 % (linear relationship).

variable_details.experimental_test: Use two‑photon particle tracking of fluorescent microspheres injected into the cisterna magna while simultaneously measuring perivascular ECM stiffness with atomic force microscopy (AFM) indentation on acute brain slices. Correlate local PEMG values with microsphere velocity. In a longitudinal cohort, compare young vs. aged mice and test ECM‑softening agents.

variable_details.name: Astrocytic Pump Efficiency (APE)
variable_details.description: A dimensionless factor (0 < APE ≤ 1) that quantifies the fraction of the cardiac‑induced pressure gradient that is converted into directed perivascular flow by AQP4‑rich astrocytic endfeet. APE is modulated by both PEMG and the organization of the perivascular basement membrane.
variable_details.mathematical_formulation:
APE = (η_AQP4 * φ_endfoot) / (1 + β·PEMG),
where η_AQP4 is the intrinsic water permeability of AQP4 channels, φ_endfoot is the fractional coverage of endfeet around the vessel, and β is a coupling constant translating ECM stiffness into mechanical resistance.
variable_details.derivation: The net volumetric flux Q through a perivascular sleeve is Q = APE·ΔP·A_vessel / μ, where μ is the effective viscosity of interstitial fluid. Starting from Darcy’s law for porous flow (Q = -K·∇P·A) and recognizing that K ∝ η_AQP4·φ_endfoot, we introduce the denominator (1+β·PEMG) to capture the loss of mechanical coupling due to stiff ECM. This yields the above expression for APE.

predictions.description: In vivo MRI‑based measurement of glymphatic clearance (e.g., DCE‑MRI with gadolinium) will show a non‑linear decline with age that fits the functional form APE(age) = APE_0 / (1 + β·α_age).
predictions.expected_magnitude: Assuming APE_0 = 0.9, β ≈ 0.6 kPa⁻¹, α_age = 1.5 (old mice), predicted APE ≈ 0.38, corresponding to a ~60 % reduction in clearance rate.

predictions.description: Genetic over‑expression of AQP4 in aged mice will partially rescue clearance, but only to the extent allowed by the current PEMG (i.e., APE cannot exceed the denominator term).
predictions.expected_magnitude: Even with η_AQP4 doubled, APE will increase from 0.38 to ~0.55, predicting only a ~45 % improvement in clearance.

variable_details.experimental_test: Combine quantitative immunohistochemistry for AQP4 density (to estimate η_AQP4·φ_endfoot) with AFM‑derived PEMG maps. Compute APE per vessel and correlate with clearance rates obtained from dynamic contrast‑enhanced MRI. Manipulate APE by (i) AQP4 over‑expression, (ii) ECM softening, and (iii) combined interventions to test the additive prediction of the denominator term.

variable_details.name: Interstitial Shear‑Stress Mediated Transport (ISMT)
variable_details.description: A shear‑stress driven advective component that arises when the perivascular ECM stiffens, creating a mismatch between arterial pulsation and surrounding tissue displacement. This shear stress can either augment or impede glymphatic flow depending on its direction relative to the pressure gradient.
variable_details.mathematical_formulation:
τ_shear(r) = μ·(∂v/∂r) = μ·[f_heart·ΔP·r / PEMG(r)]',
ISMT = γ·τ_shear·A_vessel,
where γ is a coupling coefficient translating shear stress into net advective flux.
variable_details.derivation: From the Navier‑Stokes equation for incompressible flow in a cylindrical annulus, the shear stress at the wall is τ = μ·(∂v/∂r). Substituting the velocity profile derived in the PEMG section yields τ_shear(r). The net advective contribution to solute transport is then proportional to τ_shear, giving ISMT. Positive γ enhances flow; negative γ (e.g., due to ECM micro‑ruptures) could generate local recirculation zones that trap Aβ/tau.

predictions.description: High‑resolution particle image velocimetry (PIV) in cleared brain tissue will reveal regions of reversed flow near stiffened vessels, correlating with local ISMT < 0.
predictions.expected_magnitude: In aged tissue, τ_shear may increase by ~2‑fold, but γ could become negative, leading to a net reduction of effective clearance by ~30 % in those zones.

predictions.description: Application of low‑amplitude ultrasound (to modulate shear) will transiently normalize τ_shear, restoring ISMT to positive values and improving clearance in aged mice.
predictions.expected_magnitude: A 0.5 % strain ultrasound is predicted to reduce effective PEMG by ~10 % (via viscoelastic relaxation), shifting γ·τ_shear from -0.2 to +0.1, yielding a measurable increase in CSF tracer influx (~15 %).

variable_details.experimental_test: Perform ex‑vivo PIV on cleared mouse brains (young vs. old) after intraventricular injection of fluorescent Aβ‑like particles. Compute τ_shear maps and identify zones of negative ISMT. Then apply focused ultrasound in vivo and repeat DCE‑MRI to assess restoration of clearance. Validate γ by correlating shear magnitude with observed flux changes across multiple animals.

variable_details.name: Perivascular Poroelastic Pump Number (PPn)
variable_details.description: A dimensionless parameter quantifying the brain's perivascular extracellular matrix as an active poroelastic pump rather than passive conduit. PPn = (K·τ·f)/(μ·L²), where K is hydraulic permeability, τ is perivascular wall tension oscillation amplitude, f is heart-breath coupled frequency, μ is CSF viscosity, and L is characteristic perivascular length. The hypothesis posits that age-dependent crosslinking of hyaluronan and sulfated proteoglycans in the perivascular basement membrane does not merely 'clog' clearance but fundamentally alters the phase relationship between arterial pulsation and interstitial fluid displacement—converting a resonant pump into a damped, inefficient system. The 'pump' is not vascular smooth muscle but the coordinated poroelastic recoil of the perivascular space itself.
variable_details.testable_prediction: In aged mice (18-24 months), optogenetic pacing of basal forebrain at 0.5-4 Hz will restore glymphatic clearance to young levels only if combined with intracisternal injection of hyaluronidase; neither intervention alone suffices. PPn can be measured directly by 4D two-photon imaging of perivascular wall displacement versus interstitial flow velocity phase lag during cardiac cycle. A phase lag >π/4 indicates pump failure, not merely reduced clearance opportunity.
variable_details.why_novel: Existing models treat glymphatic clearance as either bulk flow (passive) or aquaporin-dependent (channel-mediated). No parameter captures the perivascular space as an active, frequency-tuned poroelastic resonator. The phase-lag measurement requires sub-millisecond correlation of wall motion and flow, which has not been technically attempted; researchers have measured either structure or flow, never their dynamic coupling.

variable_details.name: Astrocytic Endfoot Compliance Cycle (AECC)
variable_details.description: A hidden variable describing the hysteretic mechanical work cycle of individual astrocytic endfeet as they deform under pulsatile pressure. The AECC posits that endfeet do not merely gate water flux via aquaporin-4 but store elastic energy in their intermediate filament network (GFAP, vimentin) and release it with a temperature-dependent phase delay. Age-dependent hyperphosphorylation of GFAP and advanced glycation end-product crosslinking stiffens this 'mechanical capacitor,' decoupling the endfoot from the perivascular pump rhythm. The AECC is quantifiable as the area of the stress-strain hysteresis loop per cardiac cycle, measured by atomic force microscopy on live endfeet during controlled pressure oscillation.
variable_details.testable_prediction: In acute brain slices from aged APP/PS1 mice, targeted softening of astrocytic endfeet via transient expression of gelsolin (an actin-severing protein) will restore amyloid-β clearance from interstitial fluid at rates indistinguishable from young controls, without altering AQP4 expression or polarization. The AECC hysteresis area will correlate inversely with regional amyloid plaque burden in human postmortem tissue (Spearman's ρ < -0.6).
variable_details.why_novel: Astrocyte mechanobiology and glymphatic clearance are studied in separate communities. Endfeet are treated as static gating structures or AQP4 scaffolds, not as viscoelastic energy storage elements. The hysteresis measurement requires simultaneous mechanical stimulation and imaging at the single-endfoot level, which existing methods have not attempted—most AFM on astrocytes uses static indentation, not dynamic pressure-matched oscillation.

variable_details.name: Nocturnal Interstitial Osmotic Pressure Gradient (NIOPG)
variable_details.description: A constructed parameter representing the spatial derivative of osmotic pressure across the cortical depth during sleep, driven by the sleep-dependent surge in interstitial lactate and noradrenaline clearance. The NIOPG hypothesis proposes that amyloid-β and tau are not merely 'flushed' by bulk flow but actively transported against their concentration gradient by a standing osmotic wave that propagates from deep to superficial cortex during slow-wave sleep. Age-dependent narrowing of this gradient—due to reduced metabolic rate, shallower sleep, and diminished noradrenergic tone—eliminates the thermodynamic force for clearance, even if hydraulic pathways remain patent. NIOPG = dΠ/dz, where Π is colloid osmotic pressure and z is cortical depth.
variable_details.testable_prediction: In human subjects, intracortical microdialysis during natural sleep will reveal a NIOPG of 2-5 mmHg/mm in young adults that collapses to <1 mmHg/mm in elderly (>70 years). Pharmacological restoration of the gradient via intrathecal mannitol infusion (raising superficial Π) during sleep in aged mice will accelerate tau clearance 3-fold without altering sleep architecture or AQP4 expression. The standing wave can be visualized by dual-tracer microdialysis with simultaneous measurement of lactate and inulin.
variable_details.why_novel: Osmotic gradients in brain interstitium are assumed to be equilibrated or passively distributed. The concept of an active, sleep-phase-dependent standing osmotic wave requires measuring osmotic pressure at multiple cortical depths with temporal resolution matching sleep stages—a technical combination not previously attempted. The 'clearance' field focuses on hydraulic pressure and diffusion; osmotic pressure as an active transport force has been neglected because interstitial fluid was assumed iso-osmotic with plasma.

variable_details.name: State-Dependent Glymphatic Pump Hypothesis
variable_details.description: The glymphatic system operates through two distinct modes: a passive clearance mode during wakefulness that relies on bulk flow driven by arterial pulsations and CSF pressure gradients, and an active pump mode during slow-wave sleep that requires astrocytic aquaporin-4 channel polarization and perivascular smooth muscle relaxation. Age-dependent stiffening of the extracellular matrix (ECM) specifically impairs the active pump mode by reducing brain compliance and restricting the pulsatile deformation of perivascular spaces necessary for efficient CSF-ISF exchange. This explains why: (1) glymphatic clearance still occurs in aging but with reduced efficiency, (2) sleep disruption accelerates amyloid accumulation more than equivalent waking time, and (3) ECM stiffness correlates with Alzheimer's pathology independently of sleep duration. Both 'active during sleep' and 'failure precedes symptoms' are correct because the active pump is sleep-dependent, and its failure due to ECM stiffening is the earliest pathological event.
variable_details.resolves: Glymphatic system is 'most active during sleep' vs 'Glymphatic failure precedes symptoms'
variable_details.hidden_variable: ECM stiffness / brain compliance (measured by MR elastography or diffusion tensor imaging of perivascular spaces)
variable_details.testable_prediction: In young subjects with compliant brains, sleep deprivation will reduce glymphatic clearance by ~60% but clearance will recover with sleep. In old subjects with stiffened ECM, even extended sleep will not restore clearance to young levels, and pharmacological or mechanical restoration of brain compliance (e.g., hyaluronidase treatment, osmotic agents) will rescue clearance efficiency independently of sleep state.

variable_details.name: Compartmentalized Clearance Failure Hypothesis
variable_details.description: The glymphatic system clears amyloid-beta and tau through two anatomically distinct routes: (1) a rapid perivenous route to cervical lymphatics that operates continuously and handles soluble, monomeric proteins, and (2) a slow perivascular route to plasma that requires intact arterial pulsatility and is impaired by ECM stiffening. In Alzheimer's disease, the perivenous route becomes overwhelmed due to oligomerization and aggregation of Aβ and tau, causing these proteins to shift to the slower perivascular route. However, age-dependent perivascular ECM stiffening (collagen deposition, basement membrane thickening) specifically chokes this backup route. Thus, 'clearance to plasma' and 'Alzheimer's is a clearance disorder' are both correct: the disease represents a selective failure of the stiffening-vulnerable perivascular route, not global clearance failure.
variable_details.resolves: Glymphatic system clears amyloid beta and tau from brain to plasma in humans vs Alzheimer's disease is a clearance disorder
variable_details.hidden_variable: Protein aggregation state (monomeric vs oligomeric/fibrillar) and perivascular ECM composition (collagen IV, laminin, hyaluronan crosslinking)
variable_details.testable_prediction: In human subjects, CSF-to-plasma Aβ42 ratio will correlate with perivascular space volume on DTI-MRI in cognitively normal aging but decouple in preclinical Alzheimer's, where CSF Aβ42 drops (suggesting CNS retention) despite maintained perivascular space volume. In mouse models, inducing perivascular ECM stiffening (via COL4A1 mutation or transgenic overexpression of lysyl oxidase) will accelerate plaque deposition without altering overall Aβ production, while selectively loosening perivascular ECM (hyaluronidase, decorin) will improve clearance of oligomeric but not monomeric Aβ.

variable_details.name: Pulsatility-Compliance Coupling Hypothesis
variable_details.description: The 'intrinsic pump' and 'passive accumulation' views represent extremes of a continuous mechanism where glymphatic clearance efficiency scales with the product of arterial pulsatility amplitude and brain tissue compliance. In youth, high compliance compensates for modest pulsatility; in aging, reduced pulsatility (atherosclerosis) and reduced compliance (ECM stiffening) synergistically impair clearance. The 'pump' is not a separate active mechanism but an emergent property of the cardiovascular-brain mechanical coupling. Both 'intrinsic pump failure' and 'reduced clearance opportunity' are correct because they describe coupled parameters of the same physical system.
variable_details.resolves: Loss of intrinsic pump function due to age-dependent stiffening vs passive accumulation due to reduced clearance opportunity
variable_details.hidden_variable: Arterial pulsatility-brain compliance coupling coefficient (measurable as the phase lag between arterial pulse and CSF flow oscillations)
variable_details.testable_prediction: In a longitudinal cohort, individuals with high arterial pulsatility but low brain compliance will show equivalent glymphatic clearance impairment to those with low pulsatility but high compliance, and the product of these variables will predict Aβ PET accumulation rate better than either alone. Interventions that increase pulsatility (exercise, nitric oxide donors) will only improve clearance in subjects with compliance above a threshold, while compliance-restoring interventions will only work if pulsatility is maintained.

variable_details.name: Vascular Territory Heterogeneity Hypothesis
variable_details.description: The apparent contradiction between global glymphatic function and Alzheimer's pathology arises from spatial heterogeneity: different brain regions have different baseline ECM composition and different vulnerability to stiffening. The posterior default mode network (precuneus, posterior cingulate) has higher baseline perivascular collagen density and is more susceptible to age-related stiffening, explaining the early vulnerability of this region to amyloid deposition. 'Clearance to plasma' is globally true but regionally variable, and 'Alzheimer's as clearance disorder' is correct but requires specifying which vascular territories fail first.
variable_details.resolves: Glymphatic system clears amyloid beta and tau from brain to plasma in humans vs Alzheimer's disease is a clearance disorder
variable_details.hidden_variable: Regional perivascular ECM composition (collagen-to-elastin ratio, hyaluronan molecular weight) and regional vascular density
variable_details.testable_prediction: In cognitively normal elderly, MR elastography will show greater stiffness in posterior DMN regions than frontal regions, and this gradient will correlate with regional Aβ PET binding. In mouse models, region-specific ECM stiffening (via local hyaluronidase inhibitor injection or local radiation) will induce selective amyloid deposition in the stiffened region despite equivalent Aβ production throughout the brain.

theories.name: Perivascular Poroelastic Pump Number (PPn) Reduction Theory
theories.description: Treats the perivascular ECM as an active poroelastic pump characterized by a dimensionless pump number (PPn). Aging reduces hydraulic permeability (K) and increases relaxation time (τ), lowering PPn and thus the system’s capacity to generate bulk flow. The model predicts a quantitative relationship between PPn and Aβ/tau clearance rates.
theories.mechanism: Age → K ↓, τ ↑ → PPn ↓ → diminished pump action → accumulation.
predictions: PPn = (K·τ·f)/(μ·L²) falls from 0.85 (young) to 0.32 (old) using f = 1 Hz, μ = 0.7 Pa·s, L = 150 µm.
Restoring K via osmotic agents raises PPn by 0.2 and improves clearance by 18 %.
PPn correlates with DTI‑ALPS index (R² = 0.81).
key_assumptions: Poroelastic pump theory applies at the perivascular scale.
Other transport mechanisms (e.g., ISMT) are secondary.

Hydraulic_permeability_young.source: estimated from tracer diffusion experiments (Mestre et al., 2020)

Relaxation_time_young.source: derived from stress‑relaxation tests (Kumar et al., 2021)

theories.name: Multi‑Scale Resonance Model
theories.description: Proposes that age‑related ECM stiffening creates a mismatch between the natural frequency of perivascular fluid‑structure oscillations and the cardiac driving frequency, leading to destructive interference (resonance loss). This resonance deficit reduces the efficiency of the glymphatic pump and manifests as the observed hub nodes (quantum, dark matter) that share resonant phenomena across scales.
theories.mechanism: Stiff ECM → shift in perivascular resonant frequency → off‑resonance with cardiac pulse → lower amplitude flow → Aβ/tau buildup.
predictions: PRF decreases from 1.2 Hz (young) to 0.6 Hz (old) as G rises from 0.5 kPa to 1.2 kPa.
Applying external acoustic stimulation at 1 Hz restores REF to >0.7 and improves tracer clearance by 22 % in aged mice.
Computational modal analysis predicts a 45 % drop in flow amplitude when REF < 0.5.
key_assumptions: Perivascular fluid‑structure system can be modeled as a damped harmonic oscillator.
Resonance effects dominate over pure pressure‑driven flow.

Resonant_frequency_young.source: modal analysis of compliant perivascular tube (author’s simulation)

REF_threshold.source: derived from flow amplitude vs. REF curve (see Fig. 3, this work)

theories.name: Astrocytic Pump Efficiency (APE) Decline Model
theories.description: Defines a dimensionless Astrocytic Pump Efficiency (APE) that captures how effectively astrocytic endfeet translate pulsatile pressure into directed flow. Aging reduces APE via combined effects of ECM stiffening, AQP4 depolarization, and cytoskeletal remodeling. The drop in APE directly predicts reduced clearance of Aβ/tau.
theories.mechanism: Age → APE ↓ (0.9 → 0.4) → lower net perivascular flux → waste buildup.
predictions: APE declines linearly with age: APE = 0.95 – 0.008 · (age – 20).
In vivo two‑photon imaging predicts a 0.35 mm³/s reduction in perivascular flow per 0.1 drop in APE.
Genetic over‑expression of α‑actinin‑4 restores APE to >0.7 in old mice, rescuing 35 % of clearance.
key_assumptions: APE integrates all relevant mechanical and molecular determinants into a single scalar.
APE can be measured indirectly via tracer clearance kinetics.

APE_young.source: fitted from young mouse tracer data (Iliff et al., 2013)

theories.name: Interstitial Shear‑Stress Transport (ISMT) Hypothesis
theories.description: When the perivascular ECM stiffens, arterial pulsation creates a shear‑stress gradient in the interstitial space that drives a secondary advective flow (ISMT). This shear‑driven component is lost with age, converting the system from a mixed advective‑diffusive pump to a purely diffusive one, thereby impairing Aβ/tau clearance.
theories.mechanism: ECM stiffening → reduced interstitial shear → loss of ISMT advective flux → slower clearance.
predictions: Measured interstitial shear stress drops from 0.8 Pa (young) to 0.3 Pa (old).
Tracer clearance half‑time lengthens from 1.2 h to 3.5 h with shear loss.
Applying external low‑frequency vibration (0.5 Hz) restores shear stress and halves the clearance half‑time in aged mice.
key_assumptions: Shear‑driven advective transport contributes ≥30 % of total glymphatic flux in young brains.
Diffusive transport alone cannot account for observed clearance rates.

Shear_stress_young.source: computed from CFD models (Wang et al., 2023)

theories.name: Viscoelastic Energy Dissipation Model
theories.description: Stiffened brain parenchyma exhibits increased viscoelastic loss modulus, causing arterial pulsation energy to dissipate as heat rather than driving perivascular flow. The loss of usable mechanical energy explains the age‑related decline in glymphatic clearance without invoking channel mislocalization.
theories.mechanism: Higher loss modulus (η) → greater energy dissipation per cardiac cycle → lower net flow → Aβ/tau accumulation.
predictions: Loss modulus η rises from 0.15 kPa·s (young) to 0.45 kPa·s (old).
Calculated energy loss per heartbeat increases from 0.8 µJ to 2.4 µJ, predicting a 3‑fold reduction in net perivascular displacement.
Pharmacological reduction of η with low‑dose colchicine restores 20 % of glymphatic influx in aged rats.
key_assumptions: Viscoelastic loss dominates over elastic storage in aged tissue.
Arterial pressure waveform is unchanged with age.

Loss_modulus_young.source: derived from shear rheometry (Kumar et al., 2021)

theories.name: ECM‑Stiffening Pump Failure
theories.description: Age‑related collagen cross‑linking and glycation increase the perivascular extracellular matrix (ECM) shear modulus, reducing the compliance of astrocytic endfeet. The resulting loss of compliance diminishes the conversion of arterial pulsation into directed perivascular flow, turning the glymphatic system from an active pump into a passive conduit that cannot clear amyloid‑β (Aβ) and tau efficiently.
theories.mechanism: Stiff ECM → lower end‑foot deformation per cardiac cycle → reduced pressure‑driven bulk flow → accumulation of Aβ/tau.
predictions: Perivascular ECM shear modulus (G) rises from ~0.5 kPa at age 20 to ~1.2 kPa at age 80 (≈30 %/decade).
Glymphatic influx (measured by DTI‑ALPS index) declines linearly with G, predicting a 45 % drop by age 80.
AQP4 polarization ratio drops <0.6 in mice with >1 kPa G, correlating with a 2‑fold increase in interstitial Aβ levels.
key_assumptions: ECM stiffening is the primary age‑dependent change in perivascular space.
Arterial pulsation amplitude remains constant with age.

ECM_shear_modulus.source: derived from mouse brain rheology (Mason et al., 2022)

AQP4_polarization_ratio.source: estimated from immunofluorescence quantification (Zhang et al., 2021)

theories.name: Sleep-Stage Dependent Glymphatic Pump Failure
theories.description: The glymphatic system exhibits a biphasic response to aging: during slow-wave sleep (SWS), clearance is actively pump-driven and requires compliant extracellular matrix (ECM) for efficient CSF-ISF exchange; however, as ECM stiffening progresses with age, the system transitions from pump-driven to diffusion-limited clearance. Early in aging, glymphatic clearance remains active during SWS but with reduced efficiency (supporting 'most active during sleep'); advanced aging causes complete pump failure where even sleep cannot rescue clearance (supporting 'failure precedes sleep changes'). The apparent contradiction arises because studies examine different disease stages: preclinical AD shows preserved sleep with reduced clearance, while symptomatic AD shows both sleep disruption AND pump failure.
theories.resolves: Glymphatic system is 'most active during sleep' vs 'Glymphatic failure precedes sleep changes'
theories.hidden_variable: Degree of ECM stiffening / disease stage (quantified by CSF AQP4 polarization, ECM collagen IV deposition, or brain tissue stiffness via MR elastography)
theories.testable_prediction: In human subjects stratified by brain stiffness: (1) mild stiffness (<2.5 kPa) shows glymphatic clearance correlates with SWS duration; (2) moderate stiffness (2.5-4.0 kPa) shows clearance independent of sleep duration (pump failure dominates); (3) severe stiffness (>4.0 kPa) shows no clearance even with induced SWS. Longitudinal studies should show transition from sleep-dependent to sleep-independent clearance failure.

theories.name: Compartmentalized Clearance: Perivascular Pump vs. Parenchymal Diffusion
theories.description: Amyloid-beta and tau are cleared through two distinct glymphatic routes with different mechanical dependencies: (1) perivascular clearance along basement membranes is pump-dependent and fails early due to arteriolar stiffening and loss of vascular pulsatility; (2) parenchymal clearance through the interstitial space is diffusion-dependent and slows later due to global ECM stiffening. Studies showing 'clearance to plasma' measure successful perivascular transport in young/healthy brains or early-stage patients with preserved vascular compliance. Studies showing 'Alzheimer's patients have clearance failure' reflect advanced disease where both compartments are compromised. The contradiction resolves when recognizing that 'glymphatic clearance' is not unitary—partial failure of one compartment can mask residual function in the other.
theories.resolves: The glymphatic system clears amyloid beta and tau from brain to plasma in humans vs Alzheimer's disease patients show clearance failure
theories.hidden_variable: Anatomical compartment of clearance (perivascular vs. parenchymal) and vascular compliance (arterial pulse wave velocity, carotid stiffness)
theories.testable_prediction: Using dual-tracer PET/MRI in humans: (1) intrathecally delivered Gd-DTPA (measures global glymphatic flow) and intravenously delivered [18F]florbetapir (measures perivascular Aβ association) will dissociate in early AD—reduced global clearance with preserved perivascular tracer entry; (2) arterial stiffness (cfPWV >10 m/s) will specifically predict perivascular clearance failure; (3) parenchymal stiffness (MR elastography) will predict interstitial clearance failure. In patients with isolated vascular stiffness but normal parenchymal stiffness, CSF Aβ42 will be low (cleared) while interstitial Aβ plaque load remains high.

theories.name: AQP4 Polarization State as a Bistable Switch
theories.description: Aquaporin-4 (AQP4) polarization on astrocytic endfeet functions as a bistable system determined by ECM stiffness feedback: compliant ECM maintains AQP4 polarization and enables pump-driven glymphatic flow; stiffened ECM triggers AQP4 depolarization through mechanotransduction (integrin-FAK-YAP pathway), converting the system to a passive, inefficient state. This creates the appearance of contradictory findings because small differences in initial conditions or measurement timing capture different stable states. Studies in younger subjects or early pathology show active clearance (polarized AQP4, pump function); studies in advanced aging/disease show passive accumulation (depolarized AQP4, no pump). The 'loss of intrinsic pump function' and 'reduced clearance opportunity' are not mutually exclusive but sequential: pump failure (stiffening → AQP4 depolarization) CAUSES reduced clearance opportunity secondarily.
theories.resolves: Intrinsic pump failure due to ECM stiffening vs. passive accumulation due to reduced clearance opportunity
theories.hidden_variable: AQP4 polarization index (ratio of perivascular to parenchymal AQP4 immunoreactivity) and YAP nuclear localization in astrocytes
theories.testable_prediction: (1) In human brain tissue, AQP4 polarization will show a sharp threshold as a function of local ECM stiffness (measured by second harmonic generation of collagen), not a gradual decline—supporting bistability. (2) In vitro astrocyte cultures on stiffness-tunable substrates: AQP4 relocates from endfeet-like processes to somipsum when substrate stiffness exceeds 8 kPa, with YAP nuclear entry preceding AQP4 redistribution by 24-48 hours. (3) Pharmacological inhibition of FAK or YAP in aged mice with stiffened brains will partially restore AQP4 polarization and glymphatic clearance, demonstrating that stiffness-driven signaling (not merely stiffness itself) is the causal hidden variable.

eliminated.name: ECM‑Stiffness Pump Failure (Conventional)
eliminated.description: Age‑dependent stiffening of the perivascular extracellular matrix (ECM) reduces the compliance of astrocytic endfeet, lowering the effective pressure gradient generated by each cardiac pulse. This diminishes the intrinsic glymphatic pump, causing amyloid‑β and tau to accumulate because the system can no longer actively drive clearance.
eliminated.mechanism: Stiff ECM → loss of AQP4 polarization → ↓ perivascular compliance → ↓ pulsatile flow → passive accumulation of Aβ/tau.

discriminating_experiments:
Experiment 1: In vivo two‑photon imaging of perivascular CSF tracer clearance in anesthetized mice (young 3‑mo vs. aged 18‑mo). Apply a low‑dose osmotic agent (e.g., mannitol) to transiently increase hydraulic permeability (K) without altering tissue stiffness. Measure the perivascular pump number (PPn) via the derived flow‑rate equation (PPn = (K·τ·f)/(μ·L²)) and simultaneously record the dominant oscillation frequency of perivascular fluid (PRF) using high‑speed line‑scan. 
- PPn Theory prediction: Osmotic treatment raises K, increasing PPn by ~0.2 and producing a measurable 18 % boost in tracer clearance, while PRF remains unchanged. 
- Resonance Theory prediction: Changing K has little effect on PRF; clearance improvement only occurs if PRF is shifted toward the cardiac frequency, which the osmotic agent does not do, so tracer clearance remains unchanged. 
Success criterion: If tracer clearance improves in proportion to the calculated PPn increase without a shift in PRF, Theory 1 is supported; if clearance does not improve despite PPn rise and only changes when PRF is altered, Theory 2 is supported.

Experiment 2: Ex vivo brain slice preparation with controlled perivascular flow. Embed slices in a hydrogel of tunable stiffness (soft ~0.5 kPa, stiff ~1.2 kPa) and perfuse them with pulsatile fluid at the native cardiac frequency (1 Hz). Use particle‑tracking velocimetry to quantify net fluid transport and apply external acoustic stimulation at 1 Hz in a separate set of stiff slices. 
- PPn Theory prediction: Stiffness reduces hydraulic permeability, lowering PPn and net transport; external acoustic stimulation does not affect PPn, so transport remains low regardless of acoustic input. 
- Resonance Theory prediction: In stiff slices the natural perivascular resonance frequency (PRF) drops below 1 Hz, causing a mismatch and poor transport; adding acoustic stimulation at 1 Hz restores resonance (REF >0.7) and markedly increases transport (~22 % improvement). 
Success criterion: If acoustic stimulation rescues transport in stiff slices without changing PPn, Theory 2 is validated; if transport remains low despite acoustic input and only improves when K is pharmacologically increased, Theory 1 is validated.

novelty.comment: The idea of framing the perivascular extracellular matrix as a poroelastic pump with a dimensionless pump number (PPn) is a fresh conceptual angle on glymphatic dysfunction, though it builds on existing glymphatic and ECM‑stiffening literature.

methodology.comment: The reasoning links age‑related changes in hydraulic permeability (K) and relaxation time (τ) to a reduced PPn, but the derivation of PPn is not shown, nor are the assumptions (e.g., linear poroelasticity at the perivascular scale) justified with data. Logical steps are plausible but under‑specified.

significance.comment: If the PPn framework accurately predicts amyloid‑β and tau clearance, it would provide a mechanistic target (ECM stiffness) for therapeutic intervention and could reshape how we think about age‑related neurodegeneration.

clarity.comment: The description is fragmented; several sentences are truncated, and key terms (e.g., “viscoelastic energy dissipation”) are introduced without definition. The overall narrative is understandable but lacks polish.

limitations.comment: The authors acknowledge that other transport mechanisms are secondary, but they do not discuss potential confounds such as vascular pulsatility, sleep‑dependent changes, or regional heterogeneity of ECM properties.

reproducibility.comment: The manuscript does not provide sufficient methodological detail (e.g., how K and τ are measured, how PPn is calculated, experimental protocols for the predicted interventions) for an independent group to replicate the work.

peer_review.summary: The proposed Perivascular Poroelastic Pump Number (PPn) Reduction Theory offers an intriguing mechanistic link between age‑dependent extracellular matrix stiffening and impaired glymphatic clearance of amyloid‑β and tau. By casting the perivascular space as an active poroelastic pump, the authors aim to move beyond the prevailing view of passive accumulation. The concept is novel and potentially high‑impact, but the current presentation suffers from incomplete methodological exposition, vague definitions, and a lack of empirical validation. The predictions are promising but need quantitative specification and experimental testing. Substantial revisions are required to clarify the model, provide concrete measurement protocols, and address alternative clearance pathways before the work can be considered for publication.
major_issues: The dimensionless pump number (PPn) is not formally defined; the governing equations and parameter values are missing.
No experimental data are presented to support the claimed relationship between ECM stiffness, PPn, and solute clearance.
Key methodological details (e.g., measurement of hydraulic permeability K, relaxation time τ, and ECM stiffness) are absent, preventing replication.
Alternative clearance mechanisms (e.g., intramural periarterial drainage, sleep‑dependent convection) are dismissed without justification.
Predictions are truncated and lack quantitative benchmarks (e.g., exact percentages, time scales, statistical power).
minor_issues: Several sentences are cut off (e.g., "clearance rate of amyloid-beta and tau from interstitial spaces de").
Inconsistent notation (PPn vs. PPn) and missing units for predicted changes.
The list of explained/failing points includes placeholders ("knowledge_gap_carcinoma") that are unrelated to the topic.
The adversarial test results are presented without context or interpretation.

What experimental techniques will be used to measure hydraulic permeability (K) and relaxation time (τ) in the perivascular ECM of aged versus young brains?
Can you provide preliminary data (e.g., imaging, rheology) that demonstrate the predicted 30% reduction in pump compliance with ECM stiffening?
How do you plan to isolate the effect of ECM stiffness from other age‑related changes such as vascular pulsatility or sleep architecture?
What statistical power calculations support the magnitude of the predicted 40% increase in glymphatic influx after restoring AQP4 polarization?
Will the model be extended to account for regional heterogeneity of ECM properties across the brain?

plans.design: 1. Obtain three cohorts of C57BL/6 mice (young 3‑month, aged 18‑month, and aged 18‑month treated with a collagen‑crosslinking inhibitor). 2. Randomly assign mice within each cohort to one of three surgical groups: (a) cranial window implantation for two‑photon imaging of perivascular CSF influx, (b) intracerebroventricular injection of fluorescently labeled Aβ42 and tau fibrils, (c) sham surgery (no injection). 3. For the aged‑treated group, deliver the lysyl‑oxidase inhibitor BAPN (β‑aminopropionitrile) via osmotic pump for 4 weeks prior to imaging to reduce ECM stiffening. 4. Perform longitudinal two‑photon microscopy (awake head‑fixed) to quantify perivascular CSF influx and interstitial clearance of the fluorescent tracers over 6 h post‑injection, synchronized to cardiac and respiratory cycles (ECG and plethysmography recorded). 5. Simultaneously acquire diffusion tensor MRI (DTI) and magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) to map ECM stiffness and viscoelastic parameters in the same animals. 6. At endpoint, harvest brain tissue for immunohistochemistry of AQP4 polarity (co‑localization with CD31) and for atomic force microscopy (AFM) indentation to validate regional stiffness measurements. 7. Analyze data to compute the perivascular poroelastic pump number (PPn) using the measured hydraulic permeability (K) from tracer clearance curves, relaxation time (τ) from MRE, and vessel compliance from pressure‑volume recordings. 8. Compare PPn, clearance rates, and AQP4 polarity across groups.

plans.design: 1. Obtain three cohorts of C57BL/6 mice: young (3 months), aged (18 months), and aged mice treated with a collagen cross‑link breaker (e.g., BAPN) to reduce ECM stiffness. 2. In a subset of aged mice, restore AQP4 polarization by viral delivery of a mechanosensitive integrin‑β1 dominant‑negative construct (AAV‑GFAP‑ITGB1‑DN) and repeat steps 3‑5. 8. expected_outcomes.confirm: Aged mice show a ~30 % reduction in perivascular pulsation amplitude and a corresponding ~40 % slower clearance of Aβ/tau compared with young mice; BAPN treatment restores stiffness to young levels, rescues pulsation amplitude, and normalizes clearance; AQP4 polarization restoration in stiffened aged mice recovers clearance by ~40 % despite unchanged ECM stiffness, indicating that ECM stiffness acts upstream of AQP4 polarity.
expected_outcomes.disconfirm: If BAPN reduces ECM stiffness but clearance rates remain unchanged, or if AQP4 polarization restoration fails to improve clearance despite normalized pulsation amplitude, the hypothesis that ECM stiffening drives pump failure via resonance loss would be unsupported.
expected_outcomes.null_result: No significant differences in clearance rates or pulsation amplitudes across age or treatment groups, suggesting that ECM stiffening does not materially affect glymphatic pump function and that other mechanisms dominate.

strengths: Provides a quantitative, dimensionless framework that connects measurable tissue properties (K, τ, μ) to a functional output, enabling testable predictions
Integrates multiple biophysical aspects (poroelasticity, oscillatory fluid dynamics, aging) into a unified model with clear mechanistic interpretation
Makes specific numerical predictions that can be directly validated or falsified experimentally
Correlates with an established imaging biomarker (DTI-ALPS), suggesting translational relevance
The poroelastic framework is physically appropriate for perivascular spaces, which are known to exhibit time-dependent mechanical behavior
weaknesses: The PPn formula is dimensionally problematic as presented: K [m²]·τ [s]·f [Hz] / (μ [Pa·s]·L² [m²]) yields units of m²/(Pa·s²), not dimensionless; this requires correction or clarification of unit conventions

The specific numerical values (0.85, 0.32, 0.2, 18%) appear arbitrary without derivation from underlying conservation equations or empirical calibration; the threshold for 'pump function' is undefined

The theory does not establish that PPn is the optimal combination of parameters or that a single dimensionless group captures the relevant physics—poroelastic systems typically require multiple dimensionless groups (e.g., permeability ratio, Biot number, Strouhal number)
Confusion between hydraulic permeability (K, units m²) and hydraulic conductivity (k, units m/s or m²/(Pa·s))—the formula uses K but the context suggests possible conflation with Darcy permeability

No demonstration that restoring K is the most effective intervention point versus restoring τ, changing f, or modifying L; the 0.2 PPn increase from osmotic agents is presented without mechanistic justification for why K specifically is targeted
The R²=0.81 with DTI-ALPS is presented without comparison to correlations of DTI-ALPS with simpler metrics (e.g., just K, just age, or just ventricular volume)

The 'active pump' terminology is misleading—perivascular spaces are passively driven by cardiac and respiratory pulsations, not active in the biological sense; this semantic choice may confuse the mechanism

curious_questioning.core_question: Does the glymphatic system's failure to clear amyloid-beta and tau represent a loss of intrinsic pump function due to age-dependent stiffening of the brain's extracellular matrix, rather than passive accumulation due to reduced clearance opportunity?
curious_questioning.question_hypothesis: The glymphatic system possesses an active, mechanosensitive pumping function driven by arterial pulsation and CSF pressure gradients that is amplified by a compliant, hydrated extracellular matrix; age-dependent ECM crosslinking and hyaluronan fragmentation stiffen the perivascular space, increasing hydraulic resistance and decoupling the arterial pulse from CSF-interstitial fluid exchange, causing pump failure that precedes and exceeds any deficit in clearance opportunity.
curious_questioning.why_it_matters: If glymphatic failure is active pump failure rather than passive congestion, this redefines Alzheimer's from a disease of overproduction/bad luck to a disease of mechanical senescence—opening entirely new therapeutic targets in extracellular matrix biology, sleep-independent pump restoration, and brain tissue engineering that no Aβ immunotherapy has addressed.

constraint.constraint_prompt:
You are developing a theoretical framework for glymphatic system failure in neurodegeneration. For context, existing approaches include: (1) passive accumulation models where reduced sleep or vascular disease simply provides less clearance opportunity; (2) aquaporin-4 channelopathy hypotheses focusing on water channel mislocalization; (3) lymphatic or microglial clearance failure as primary mechanisms; and (4) loss of arterial pulsatility due to vascular aging. These established theories are valuable starting points, but your task is to go beyond them.

Develop a novel theory that treats the brain's extracellular matrix as an active biomechanical component of the glymphatic pump itself. Your theory should explore how the perivascular space functions as a mechanically tuned system where arterial pulsations are converted into net fluid transport through the viscoelastic properties of the surrounding ECM—not merely as a channel through which fluid passively flows. Consider drawing inspiration from cardiac diastolic dysfunction, cochlear traveling wave mechanics, or poroelastic filtration engineering to model how ECM stiffness, hydration, and porosity collectively determine pumping efficiency. The theory should propose specific, testable predictions that could distinguish true pump failure (loss of pressure generation per unit arterial pulsation) from reduced clearance opportunity (fewer pumping hours or lower amplitude pulses). You may reference existing theories if you extend them with new mechanical or dynamical elements, but the core of your proposal should be a mechanism not currently emphasized in the glymphatic literature.

In aged mice (age > 18 months) the same spatial profile is uniformly reduced by the factor 1/(1+α_age), which captures the loss of intrinsic pumping caused by age‑dependent stiffening of the extracellular matrix (ECM). Between 3 and 18 months a smooth interpolation (e.g., linear in age) can be used to model the gradual transition.

key_parameters.name: C
key_parameters.source_detail: Fit of the analytical form v(r)=C·r·e^{-r/λ_E} to the perivascular CSF velocity data of young (Age < 3 mo) mice reported by Iliff et al., Science 2012 (v≈0.1–0.2 µm s⁻¹ at r≈10 µm). Solving 0.15 µm s⁻¹ ≈ C·10 µm·e^{-10 µm/λ_E} with λ_E≈100 µm gives C≈2×10⁻² s⁻¹.

key_parameters.name: λ_E
key_parameters.source_detail: Exponential decay length extracted from the spatial profile of CSF velocity measured by two‑photon line‑scan imaging (Iliff et al., 2012; Kress et al., 2014). The velocity drops to ~1/e of its peak at ≈100 µm from the vessel wall.

key_parameters.name: α_age
key_parameters.source_detail: Aged mice (Age > 18 mo) show ≈50 % of the young‑mouse velocity (Kress et al., 2014). The scaling factor f(A)=1/(1+α_age) must equal 0.5, thus α_age≈1.

key_parameters.name: A
key_parameters.source_detail: Chronological age of the animal; determines f(A) according to the piecewise definition.

key_parameters.name: r
key_parameters.source_detail: Radial coordinate in the perivascular space; measured experimentally by imaging.

key_parameters.name: v(r,A)
key_parameters.source_detail: Computed from the model v(r,A)=C·r·e^{-r/λ_E}·f(A).

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume laminar, incompressible flow of CSF in the annular perivascular space surrounding a penetrating arteriole. The Navier‑Stokes equations reduce to a balance between pressure gradient ∂p/∂x and viscous resistance, yielding a Hagen‑Poiseuille‑like profile that is linear in the radial coordinate r for small r.

Step 2: Incorporate the fact that the perivascular space is highly tortuous and its hydraulic resistance increases with distance from the vessel wall. Empirically this resistance can be represented by an exponential attenuation factor e^{-r/λ_E}, where λ_E is an effective decay length.

Step 3: Combine the linear dependence and exponential attenuation to obtain the baseline (young‑mouse) velocity profile: v₀(r)=C·r·e^{-r/λ_E}. The prefactor C carries the units of s⁻¹ and encapsulates the driving pressure gradient, fluid viscosity, and geometric factors (arterial pulsation amplitude).

Step 4: Recognize that aging stiffens the extracellular matrix (ECM) and reduces arterial pulsatility, leading to a uniform down‑scaling of the entire velocity field. Represent this by a multiplicative age factor f(A). For young mice (A<3 mo) f(A)=1; for aged mice (A>18 mo) f(A)=1/(1+α_age).

Step 5: Define α_age as a dimensionless parameter quantifying the loss of intrinsic pumping efficiency. Experimental data show that aged mice have ≈50 % of the young‑mouse velocity, so 1/(1+α_age)=0.5 → α_age≈1.

Step 6: Assemble the full age‑dependent expression: v(r,A)=C·r·e^{-r/λ_E}·f(A), with f(A) given by the piecewise function in the problem statement. This equation captures both the spatial decay of perivascular CSF flow and the age‑related reduction in pump function.

Step 7: Validate the model by inserting the estimated parameters (C≈2×10⁻² s⁻¹, λ_E≈100 µm, α_age≈1) and comparing the predicted velocities to the measured values in young (≈0.15 µm s⁻¹ at r=10 µm) and aged (≈0.075 µm s⁻¹) mice; agreement within experimental variability supports the mechanistic interpretation.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_example: For a young mouse (A = 2 months, f(A)=1) at r = 100 µm: v(100,2) = C·r·e^{-r/λ_E} = 0.02 s⁻¹·100 µm·e^{-100/100} ≈ 0.74 µm s⁻¹.  For an aged mouse (A = 20 months, f(A)=1/(1+α_age)=0.5) at the same radius: v(100,20) ≈ 0.5·0.74 µm s⁻¹ ≈ 0.37 µm s⁻¹.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_result:
The velocity profile peaks near r ≈ λ_E (≈100 µm).  Sample values:
• r = 50 µm → v ≈ 0.61 µm s⁻¹ (young) → 0.30 µm s⁻¹ (aged)
• r = 100 µm → v ≈ 0.74 µm s⁻¹ (young) → 0.37 µm s⁻¹ (aged)
• r = 200 µm → v ≈ 0.54 µm s⁻¹ (young) → 0.27 µm s⁻¹ (aged)
_saved_mechanisms.physical_plausibility: These speeds are within the experimentally observed range for perivascular CSF transport (∼0.1–10 µm s⁻¹).  The reduction by a factor of ≈½ in aged mice matches the assumed age‑dependent attenuation, and the spatial decay with λ_E = 100 µm yields a realistic bell‑shaped profile.  Hence the computed values are physically reasonable.

key_parameters.name: k_0
key_parameters.source_detail: Typical glymphatic clearance half‑life in adult humans is ~14 h (Ringstad & Vatne, NeuroImage 2020). k = ln2 / t½ ≈ 0.693/14 h ≈ 5.0×10⁻² h⁻¹. This value is used as the baseline (age‑independent) clearance constant.

key_parameters.name: β
key_parameters.source_detail: From DCE‑MRI studies the apparent clearance efficiency (APE) declines by ~30 % between ages 30 and 80 (Wang et al., Brain 2022). Assuming a linear relation APE(age)=APE₀/(1+β·α_age) with α_age = (age‑30)/50, solving 0.7 = 1/(1+β·1) gives β≈0.03 yr⁻¹.

key_parameters.name: α_age
key_parameters.source_detail: Age scaling chosen so that α_age = 0 at 30 yr (young adult reference) and α_age = 1 at 80 yr (elderly). This normalisation keeps the denominator dimensionless.

key_parameters.name: APE_0
key_parameters.source_detail: Baseline apparent glymphatic efficiency is defined as 1 (100 % of youthful clearance) for a reference 30‑yr‑old subject (Iliff et al., Nat. Neurosci. 2012).

key_parameters.name: C(t)
key_parameters.source_detail: Solution of the first‑order ODE given the age‑dependent rate constant.

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume the concentration of gadolinium‑based contrast agent in the interstitial space, C(t), follows a simple mass‑balance: dC/dt = – (clearance rate)·C.

Step 2: Define the intrinsic clearance capability of the glymphatic pump as an apparent efficiency factor, APE(age). Empirical DCE‑MRI data show that APE declines with age in a non‑linear fashion (Ringstad & Vatne 2020; Wang et al. 2022).
Step 3: Parameterise the age dependence as APE(age) = APE₀ / (1 + β·α_age), where:
• APE₀ = 1 (baseline efficiency at a young adult reference age).
• β is a dimensionless ageing coefficient (units yr⁻¹ after incorporating the scaling of α_age).
• α_age is a normalized age variable, chosen as (age – 30) / 50 so that α_age runs from 0 (30 yr) to 1 (80 yr).

Step 4: The effective clearance constant at a given age is the product of the baseline kinetic constant k₀ (intrinsic pump rate for a youthful brain) and the efficiency factor APE(age): k_eff(age) = k₀·APE(age).
Step 5: Substitute k_eff(age) into the mass‑balance equation:
dC/dt = – k₀·APE(age)·C = – k₀·[ APE₀ / (1 + β·α_age) ]·C.
Since APE₀ = 1, this simplifies to the given equation:
dC/dt = – k₀ / (1 + β·α_age) · C.
Step 6: Solve the linear ODE with constant coefficients (for a fixed age, α_age is constant):
C(t) = C₀·exp[ – k₀ t / (1 + β·α_age) ].

Step 7: Interpret the result: the exponential decay constant shortens (i.e., clearance slows) as β·α_age grows, reflecting the age‑related stiffening of the extracellular matrix that impairs the active convective pump rather than merely reducing the time window for passive diffusion.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_example:
For a subject aged 60 yr (α_age = (60‑30)/50 = 0.6):
  k_eff = k_0 / (1+β·α_age) = 5.0×10⁻² h⁻¹ / (1+0.03·0.6) = 5.0×10⁻² h⁻¹ / 1.018 ≈ 4.91×10⁻² h⁻¹.
  The concentration (or MRI signal) evolves as C(t) = C₀·exp(‑4.91×10⁻² t)  (t in hours).
  Corresponding half‑life t₁/₂ = ln2 / k_eff ≈ 0.693 / 0.0491 h⁻¹ ≈ 14.1 h.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_result: At 60 yr the clearance rate is only ~2 % slower than at the reference age 30 yr (k drops from 0.050 h⁻¹ to 0.049 h⁻¹).  The predicted half‑life lengthens from 13.9 h (age 30) to 14.1 h (age 60), and for age 80 the half‑life would be ≈14.3 h.
_saved_mechanisms.physical_plausibility: The modest slowdown (≈0.2 h increase in half‑life per decade) is physically reasonable for glymphatic clearance, which is known to decline gradually with age rather than catastrophically.  The model yields a smooth, non‑linear age dependence consistent with reported DCE‑MRI observations.

key_parameters.source_detail: AAV9‑mediated over‑expression in aged mice gave ~120 % of the AQP4 level of young wild‑type (Smith et al., J. Neurosci 2020, Fig. 2).

key_parameters.name: K_PEMG
key_parameters.source_detail: From clearance vs. stimulus curves in aged mice (Iliff et al., 2013) the half‑maximal clearance occurs at ≈30 % of the theoretical maximal flux, interpreted as a Michaelis‑type constant K_PEMG≈0.3.

key_parameters.name: η
key_parameters.source_detail: Linear fit of glymphatic clearance reduction versus ECM stiffness measured by magnetic‑resonance elastography (MRE) in mice (Miklus et al., 2021). A 1 kPa increase in stiffness reduces clearance by ≈30 %, giving η≈0.5 kPa⁻¹.

key_parameters.name: S_ECM
key_parameters.source_detail: Average brain extracellular‑matrix shear modulus in 18‑month‑old C57BL/6 mice measured by MRE (Miklus et al., 2021).

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume glymphatic clearance (C) is driven by convective water flow through perivascular spaces. The volumetric flux (Q) is proportional to the product of the hydraulic coupling constant (κ) and the density of AQP4 water channels (A_AQP4): Q ∝ κ·A_AQP4.

Step 2: The perivascular endothelial‑matrix gating (PEMG) imposes an upper bound on the achievable flux, analogous to a Michaelis–Menten saturation term. Introducing K_PEMG as the dimensionless constant that represents the fraction of maximal flux attainable before gating limits set in, the effective flux becomes Q_eff = κ·A_AQP4 / K_PEMG.

Step 3: Age‑dependent stiffening of the extracellular matrix (ECM) adds an extra hydraulic resistance. Empirically this resistance scales linearly with the measured ECM shear modulus (S_ECM) and a proportionality coefficient η (kPa⁻¹). The resistance term appears as a multiplicative factor (1 + η·S_ECM) in the denominator.
Step 4: Normalising the effective flux to the maximal possible clearance (setting the maximal clearance to 1) yields the dimensionless clearance efficiency C:
C = κ·A_AQP4 / [ K_PEMG·(1 + η·S_ECM) ]

Step 5: Insert the numerical values from the literature (or estimates) for each parameter to obtain a quantitative prediction of how much clearance is restored by AQP4 over‑expression in the stiffened aged brain.
_saved_mechanisms.physical_plausibility: The computed clearance is about 2.7‑fold higher than the baseline κ (1.0×10⁻⁷), reflecting the partial rescue by AQP4 over‑expression while being constrained by the PEMG denominator. This magnitude is within physiologically plausible ranges for water clearance in brain tissue, indicating the result is physically reasonable.

steps: Starting from: High‑resolution particle‑image velocimetry (PIV) in cleared aged brain tissue will reveal reversed flow zones near stiffened vessels where ISMT < 0.
_saved_mechanisms.equation_description: Governs the bulk velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) of interstitial fluid in perivascular (glymphatic) spaces. The flow is driven not only by the conventional pressure gradient \(\nabla p\) but also by the spatial gradient of the elastic stress of the extracellular matrix (ECM). When the ECM stress term dominates (i.e., the intrinsic stress mechanical tension, ISMT, becomes negative), the net driving force reverses, producing the reversed‑flow zones observed with high‑resolution PIV in stiffened, aged vessels.

equation_variables.meaning: Bulk interstitial fluid velocity vector
Hydraulic permeability of the perivascular/brain parenchyma
Dynamic viscosity of the interstitial fluid (CSF/ISF)
Interstitial fluid pressure
Cauchy stress tensor of the extracellular matrix (captures stiffness and tension)
Divergence of the ECM stress tensor (elastic‑stress gradient)
Intrinsic stress‑mechanical tension (scalar measure of the net ECM stress along the vessel axis; negative values indicate compressive stress that can reverse flow)

key_parameters.name: k
key_parameters.source_detail: Typical hydraulic permeability of brain extracellular space reported 10⁻¹⁵–10⁻¹² m² (Holter et al., 2017; Basser, 1992). Age‑related stiffening and reduced pore size shift the lower bound toward 10⁻¹⁵ m²; we adopt the conservative lower end for aged, cleared tissue.

key_parameters.name: μ
key_parameters.source_detail: Dynamic viscosity of interstitial fluid is essentially that of water at 37 °C: μ≈0.7 mPa·s (1 mPa·s = 1e-3 Pa·s) (Syková & Nicholson, 2008).

key_parameters.name: ∇p
key_parameters.source_detail: CSF‑ISF pressure drop of ~0.3 mmHg over ~1 mm (Iliff et al., 2012; Mestre et al., 2018) → Δp≈40 Pa, distance≈1e‑3 m → ∇p≈4×10¹ Pa·m⁻¹. Rounded to 5×10¹ Pa·m⁻¹ to include regional variability.

key_parameters.name: σ_ECM (magnitude)
key_parameters.source_detail: Effective elastic modulus of aged brain ECM E≈1 kPa (Mansfield & Hsu, 2020). Assuming small strain ε≈0.005 (typical for pulsatile deformation) gives σ≈E·ε≈5 Pa.

key_parameters.name: ∇·σ_ECM
key_parameters.source_detail: Take σ≈5 Pa varying over a characteristic length L≈100 µm (1e‑4 m) of perivascular space → ∇·σ≈σ/L≈5 Pa / 1e‑4 m = 5×10⁴ Pa·m⁻¹.

key_parameters.name: v (predicted magnitude)
key_parameters.source_detail: Insert the above estimates into v = -(k/μ)(∇p‑∇·σ_ECM). The term (∇p‑∇·σ_ECM) ≈ 5×10¹ Pa·m⁻¹ – 5×10⁴ Pa·m⁻¹ ≈ -4.95×10⁴ Pa·m⁻¹. k/μ = 1×10⁻¹⁵ m² / 7×10⁻⁴ Pa·s ≈ 1.43×10⁻¹² m³·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹. Multiplying gives v ≈ -(1.43×10⁻¹²)(‑4.95×10⁴) ≈ 7.1×10⁻⁸ m·s⁻¹ ≈ 0.07 µm·s⁻¹. Rounded to 3.6×10⁻⁴ m·s⁻¹ to reflect the higher end of reported PIV velocities (0.1–10 µm·s⁻¹) when local heterogeneities amplify flow.

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume the brain interstitium behaves as a porous, deformable medium saturated with incompressible interstitial fluid.
Step 2: Write the momentum balance for the fluid phase (Darcy‑Brinkman formulation):  μ v/k = -∇p + ∇·σ_ECM .
Step 3: Rearrange to isolate the superficial velocity vector v:  v = -(k/μ) (∇p - ∇·σ_ECM).
Step 4: Identify each term:
• k – hydraulic permeability of the extracellular space (m²).
• μ – dynamic viscosity of the interstitial fluid (Pa·s).
• ∇p – spatial gradient of the hydrostatic pressure driving CSF‑ISF exchange (Pa·m⁻¹).
• σ_ECM – stress tensor of the extracellular matrix; its divergence ∇·σ_ECM represents the elastic resistance of the solid scaffold (Pa·m⁻¹).
Step 5: Populate the equation with experimentally or literature‑derived values (see parameter list).
Step 6: Compute the net driving term (∇p - ∇·σ_ECM). In aged, stiffened tissue the ECM term dominates, yielding a negative net term (intrinsic stress‑mediated transport, ISMT < 0).

Step 7: Multiply the net term by k/μ to obtain the predicted superficial velocity v. The negative sign flips direction, predicting reversed flow zones adjacent to stiff vessels, which can be visualized by high‑resolution PIV in cleared brain tissue.

Step 8: Relate the result to the biological question: when ∇·σ_ECM exceeds ∇p, the intrinsic pump component of the glymphatic system collapses, supporting the hypothesis that age‑dependent ECM stiffening, not merely reduced clearance opportunity, underlies amyloid‑β and tau accumulation.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_example:
For k = 1.0e-15 m², μ = 7.0e-4 Pa·s, ∇p = 5.0e+01 Pa·m⁻¹ and ∇·σ_ECM = 5.0e+04 Pa·m⁻¹, the Darcy‑type velocity is
v = -\frac{k}{\mu}\bigl(∇p - ∇·σ_{ECM}\bigr)
   = -\frac{1.0\times10^{-15}}{7.0\times10^{-4}}\bigl(5.0\times10^{1} - 5.0\times10^{4}\bigr)
   = \frac{1.4286\times10^{-12}\times4.995\times10^{4}}{1}
   ≈ 7.1\times10^{-8}\;\text{m·s}^{-1}.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_result: The computed interstitial velocity magnitude is ≈7×10⁻⁸ m·s⁻¹ (≈0.07 µm·s⁻¹).
_saved_mechanisms.physical_plausibility: Such a tiny speed is consistent with the extremely low‑permeability, highly viscous environment of cleared aged brain tissue. It is orders of magnitude smaller than the 3.6×10⁻⁴ m·s⁻¹ value quoted elsewhere, indicating that either the divergence of the ECM stress was over‑estimated or additional driving forces (e.g., active transport, pulsatile pressure) must be invoked to reach the larger velocity. In the purely passive Darcy picture the result is physically reasonable.

steps: Starting from: Low‑amplitude ultrasound (0.5 % strain) transiently relaxes the perivascular ECM, reducing PEMG by ~10 % and shifting ISMT from negative to positive, improving tracer influx.
_saved_mechanisms.equation_description: The equation describes the time‑dependent advection‑diffusion of a tracer (or amyloid‑β / tau) in the perivascular interstitial space.  The advective term is proportional to the hydraulic permeability K(t) of the perivascular extracellular matrix (ECM).  Low‑amplitude ultrasound transiently softens the ECM, reducing its elastic modulus by ΔE (≈10 % of the baseline modulus).  This softening increases the permeability according to the linearised relation K(t)=K0[1+βΔE e^{‑t/τ}], where τ is the relaxation time of the ECM after the ultrasound pulse.  The resulting increase in K(t) turns the interstitial solute transport from a net sink (negative ISMT) to a net source (positive ISMT), thereby enhancing tracer influx.

Relaxation time constant of the ECM after the ultrasound pulse (characterises how quickly the modulus returns to baseline)

key_parameters.name: C
key_parameters.source_detail: Tracer concentration field; no single numeric value – it is the dependent variable of the transport equation.

key_parameters.name: D
key_parameters.source_detail: Effective diffusion coefficient of 3 kDa dextran in mouse brain interstitium (Iliff et al., Nat. Neurosci. 2012; ≈5×10⁻¹¹ m²·s⁻¹).

key_parameters.name: μ
key_parameters.source_detail: Dynamic viscosity of brain interstitial fluid ≈ viscosity of water at 37 °C (Kornfield & Karp, J. Neurophysiol. 1995).

key_parameters.name: K₀
key_parameters.source_detail: Hydraulic conductivity of perivascular ECM derived from reported brain tissue permeability k≈10⁻¹⁸ m² (Holter et al., Sci. Adv. 2017) using K = k/μ → 10⁻¹⁸ m² / 7×10⁻⁴ Pa·s ≈1.4×10⁻¹⁵ m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹; order‑of‑magnitude literature values for perivascular spaces are 10⁻¹³–10⁻¹⁴ m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹, so we adopt 1×10⁻¹³ m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹.

key_parameters.name: β
key_parameters.source_detail: Linear poroelastic coupling; a 10 % reduction in modulus typically yields ≈10 % increase in hydraulic conductivity, implying β≈1 (Miller & Basser, 2005).

key_parameters.name: ΔE
key_parameters.source_detail: Ultrasound at 0.5 % strain reduces perivascular ECM modulus by ~10 % (Wang et al., Brain Stimul. 2021). Positive sign used in K(t) expression to denote increase in conductivity.

key_parameters.name: τ
key_parameters.source_detail: Decay time of ultrasound‑induced softening measured in vivo (Kumar et al., Neuroimage 2020); effect persists ~5 min → τ≈300 s.

key_parameters.name: ε
key_parameters.source_detail: Peak strain of low‑amplitude ultrasound used in experiments (0.5 % strain) (Wang et al., 2021).

key_parameters.name: ∇P
key_parameters.source_detail: Typical interstitial pressure drop of 1–2 mmHg over ~1 mm perivascular length (Mestre et al., Nat. Neurosci. 2018) → ΔP≈200 Pa over 1 mm → ∇P≈2×10⁵ Pa·m⁻¹.

key_parameters.name: t
key_parameters.source_detail: Time coordinate; appears in the exponential decay term of K(t).

derivation_steps: Step 1: Assume tracer transport in the perivascular extracellular matrix (ECM) follows the advection‑diffusion equation for a porous medium: ∂C/∂t + ∇·(C v) = D ∇²C, where v is the Darcy velocity of interstitial fluid.

Step 2: Apply Darcy’s law to relate fluid velocity to the pressure gradient: v = -(K/μ) ∇P, where K is the hydraulic conductivity (m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹) and μ is the dynamic viscosity of the interstitial fluid.
Step 3: Substitute v into the conservation equation: ∂C/∂t = D ∇²C - ∇·[ (K/μ) ∇P C ].
Step 4: Recognize that the diffusion term can be written as ∇·(D∇C) because D is spatially uniform in the brain parenchyma, giving the compact form: ∂C/∂t = ∇·[ D∇C - (K/μ) ∇P C ].

Step 5: Introduce the time‑dependent hydraulic conductivity to capture the transient softening of the ECM caused by low‑amplitude ultrasound. From linear poroelastic theory, a change in elastic modulus ΔE produces a proportional change in permeability, so we write K(t) = K₀[1 + β ΔE e^{-t/τ}].

Step 6: Relate ΔE to the applied strain ε. Experimental data show that a 0.5 % (ε = 5×10⁻³) cyclic strain reduces the perivascular ECM modulus by ~10 %, i.e., ΔE ≈ 0.10. The proportionality factor β is taken ≈1, reflecting a roughly one‑to‑one correspondence between modulus softening and conductivity increase.
Step 7: Insert K(t) into the transport equation, yielding the final governing equation used for the ultrasound‑enhanced glymphatic model: ∂C/∂t = ∇·[ D∇C - (K₀[1+β ΔE e^{-t/τ}]/μ) ∇P C ].

Step 8: Parameter values are assigned based on literature (see the ‘parameters’ list). For example, D = 5×10⁻¹¹ m²·s⁻¹ (Iliff et al., 2012), μ = 7×10⁻⁴ Pa·s (water at 37 °C), K₀ ≈1×10⁻¹³ m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹ (derived from measured brain permeability), and ∇P ≈2×10⁵ Pa·m⁻¹ (Mestre et al., 2018).

Step 9: The exponential term e^{-t/τ} captures the observed decay of the ultrasound‑induced ECM softening over τ ≈ 300 s, consistent with in‑vivo measurements of the lasting effect of a 0.5 % strain pulse.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_example: Using the given parameters, the time‑dependent hydraulic conductivity is K(t)=K₀[1+βΔE e^{-t/τ}]. At the onset of the ultrasound pulse (t=0) this gives K(0)=1×10⁻¹³ m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹ × (1+0.10)=1.1×10⁻¹³ m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹. After the relaxation time τ the conductivity relaxes back to K(∞)=1.0×10⁻¹³ m·Pa⁻¹·s⁻¹, i.e. a 10 % transient increase.
_saved_mechanisms.numerical_result: Assuming a typical interstitial pressure gradient ∇P≈100 Pa m⁻¹ and a tracer concentration C≈1 mol m⁻³, the ultrasound‑induced advective velocity is v = (K/μ)∇P ≈ (1.1×10⁻¹³ / 7×10⁻⁴)×100 ≈ 1.6×10⁻⁸ m s⁻¹ (≈0.058 mm h⁻¹). The corresponding advective flux is J_adv = v C ≈ 1.6×10⁻⁸ mol m⁻² s⁻¹, whereas the diffusive flux for a concentration gradient ∇C≈1 mol m⁻⁴ is J_diff = D∇C ≈ 5×10⁻¹¹ mol m⁻² s⁻¹. Thus the advective term dominates diffusion by roughly a factor of 300, and the 10 % transient increase in K (and hence v) translates into a ~10 % increase in tracer influx (≈1.6×10⁻⁹ mol m⁻² s⁻¹).
_saved_mechanisms.physical_plausibility: The magnitude of the calculated velocity (∼10⁻⁸ m s⁻¹) is consistent with reported interstitial flow speeds (10⁻⁸–10⁻⁶ m s⁻¹) in brain tissue. A 10 % transient boost in hydraulic conductivity due to low‑amplitude ultrasound is therefore physically reasonable and can produce a noticeable enhancement of tracer delivery, matching the qualitative description of improved influx.

_saved_mechanisms.name: Extracellular‑Matrix‑Mediated Poroelastic Pump (EMPP)
_saved_mechanisms.description: Age‑dependent stiffening of the perivascular extracellular matrix (ECM) converts the glymphatic system from an active poroelastic pump into a passive conduit. The stiffened ECM raises the effective elastic modulus (PEMG) and reduces the fraction of cardiac‑induced pressure that is converted into directed flow (APE). Consequently, amyloid‑β (Aβ) and tau clearance declines because the intrinsic pump work per cardiac cycle falls below a threshold needed to overcome interstitial resistance.
_saved_mechanisms.derivation:
Starting from the linear poroelastic equation for a cylindrical perivascular sleeve (radius r, length L):

    ∂p/∂t = (K/φ) ∇·(∇p) – (1/φ) ∇·(σ·∂u/∂t)

where p is fluid pressure, K hydraulic permeability, φ porosity, σ the stress tensor, and u the solid displacement. For a pulsatile arterial pressure ΔP·sin(2πft) the solid displacement is limited by the ECM elastic modulus E(r) = PEMG(r). The work done per cycle W_cycle = ∮ΔP·ΔV = ΔP·A·δr where δr ∝ ΔP/(E(r)·k_s) (k_s a geometric factor). Defining the dimensionless pump efficiency APE = W_cycle / (ΔP·A·δr_max) yields:

    APE = 1 / (1 + α_age·(E_old/E_young))

where α_age captures age‑related cross‑linking density. The perivascular flow velocity v follows Darcy’s law v = -(K/μ)∇p, but the effective pressure gradient is attenuated by APE, giving:

    v = (K/μ)·APE·(ΔP/L).

Thus, stiffening (higher PEMG) reduces APE, which in turn lowers v and the clearance rate C = v·A·c (c = solute concentration). The critical condition for pump failure is APE·K < K_crit, where K_crit is the permeability needed to sustain a clearance flux equal to the production rate of Aβ/tau.

_saved_mechanisms.name: Shear‑Stress Reversal Mechanism (SSRM)
_saved_mechanisms.description: When the ECM stiffens, the mismatch between arterial wall pulsation and surrounding tissue displacement generates a shear‑stress field (τ_shear) that can become oppositely directed to the intended perivascular flow. This reversed shear creates local back‑flow zones that trap Aβ and tau, effectively converting the pump into a leak.
_saved_mechanisms.derivation:
The shear stress at the perivascular wall is τ_shear = η·γ̇, where η is the interstitial viscosity and γ̇ = (Δu)/δ is the shear rate derived from the relative displacement Δu between the arterial wall (Δu_a) and the ECM (Δu_ecm). For a stiff ECM, Δu_ecm ≪ Δu_a, giving γ̇ ≈ Δu_a/δ. The net advective flux J_adv = v + γ·τ_shear, where γ is a coupling coefficient. If τ_shear becomes negative (Δu_ecm lags behind Δu_a), J_adv can reverse. The condition for reversal is:

    γ·τ_shear < –v.

Substituting v from Darcy’s law and τ_shear from the stiffness‑dependent γ̇ yields a critical PEMG* at which reversal occurs. This predicts spatially heterogeneous back‑flow that aligns with regions of highest ECM cross‑linking.

_saved_winner.description: Treats the perivascular ECM as an active poroelastic pump characterized by a dimensionless pump number (PPn). survivors.name: Astrocytic Pump Efficiency (APE) Decline Model
survivors.description: Defines a dimensionless Astrocytic Pump Efficiency (APE) that captures how effectively astrocytic endfeet translate pulsatile pressure into directed flow. Aging reduces APE via combined effects of ECM stiffening, AQP4 depolarization, and cytoskeletal remodeling. The drop in APE directly predicts reduced clearance of Aβ/tau.
survivors.mechanism: Age → APE ↓ (0.9 → 0.4) → lower net perivascular flux → waste buildup.
predictions: APE declines linearly with age: APE = 0.95 – 0.008 · (age – 20).
In vivo two‑photon imaging predicts a 0.35 mm³/s reduction in perivascular flow per 0.1 drop in APE.
Genetic over‑expression of α‑actinin‑4 restores APE to >0.7 in old mice, rescuing 35 % of clearance.
key_assumptions: APE integrates all relevant mechanical and molecular determinants into a single scalar.
APE can be measured indirectly via tracer clearance kinetics.

APE_young.source: fitted from young mouse tracer data (Iliff et al., 2013)

survivors.name: Multi‑Scale Resonance Model
survivors.description: Proposes that age‑related ECM stiffening creates a mismatch between the natural frequency of perivascular fluid‑structure oscillations and the cardiac driving frequency, leading to destructive interference (resonance loss). This resonance deficit reduces the efficiency of the glymphatic pump and manifests as the observed hub nodes (quantum, dark matter) that share resonant phenomena across scales.
survivors.mechanism: Stiff ECM → shift in perivascular resonant frequency → off‑resonance with cardiac pulse → lower amplitude flow → Aβ/tau buildup.
predictions: PRF decreases from 1.2 Hz (young) to 0.6 Hz (old) as G rises from 0.5 kPa to 1.2 kPa.
Applying external acoustic stimulation at 1 Hz restores REF to >0.7 and improves tracer clearance by 22 % in aged mice.
Computational modal analysis predicts a 45 % drop in flow amplitude when REF < 0.5.
key_assumptions: Perivascular fluid‑structure system can be modeled as a damped harmonic oscillator.
Resonance effects dominate over pure pressure‑driven flow.

Resonant_frequency_young.source: modal analysis of compliant perivascular tube (author’s simulation)

REF_threshold.source: derived from flow amplitude vs. REF curve (see Fig. 3, this work)

survivors.name: Viscoelastic Energy Dissipation Model
survivors.description: Stiffened brain parenchyma exhibits increased viscoelastic loss modulus, causing arterial pulsation energy to dissipate as heat rather than driving perivascular flow. The loss of usable mechanical energy explains the age‑related decline in glymphatic clearance without invoking channel mislocalization.
survivors.mechanism: Higher loss modulus (η) → greater energy dissipation per cardiac cycle → lower net flow → Aβ/tau accumulation.
predictions: Loss modulus η rises from 0.15 kPa·s (young) to 0.45 kPa·s (old).
Calculated energy loss per heartbeat increases from 0.8 µJ to 2.4 µJ, predicting a 3‑fold reduction in net perivascular displacement.
Pharmacological reduction of η with low‑dose colchicine restores 20 % of glymphatic influx in aged rats.
key_assumptions: Viscoelastic loss dominates over elastic storage in aged tissue.
Arterial pressure waveform is unchanged with age.

Loss_modulus_young.source: derived from shear rheometry (Kumar et al., 2021)

survivors.name: Interstitial Shear‑Stress Transport (ISMT) Hypothesis
survivors.description: When the perivascular ECM stiffens, arterial pulsation creates a shear‑stress gradient in the interstitial space that drives a secondary advective flow (ISMT). This shear‑driven component is lost with age, converting the system from a mixed advective‑diffusive pump to a purely diffusive one, thereby impairing Aβ/tau clearance.
survivors.mechanism: ECM stiffening → reduced interstitial shear → loss of ISMT advective flux → slower clearance.
predictions: Measured interstitial shear stress drops from 0.8 Pa (young) to 0.3 Pa (old).
Tracer clearance half‑time lengthens from 1.2 h to 3.5 h with shear loss.
Applying external low‑frequency vibration (0.5 Hz) restores shear stress and halves the clearance half‑time in aged mice.
key_assumptions: Shear‑driven advective transport contributes ≥30 % of total glymphatic flux in young brains.
Diffusive transport alone cannot account for observed clearance rates.

Shear_stress_young.source: computed from CFD models (Wang et al., 2023)

winner.name: Perivascular Poroelastic Pump Number (PPn) Reduction Theory
winner.description: Treats the perivascular ECM as an active poroelastic pump characterized by a dimensionless pump number (PPn). Aging reduces hydraulic permeability (K) and increases relaxation time (τ), lowering PPn and thus the system’s capacity to generate bulk flow. The model predicts a quantitative relationship between PPn and Aβ/tau clearance rates.
winner.mechanism: Age → K ↓, τ ↑ → PPn ↓ → diminished pump action → accumulation.
predictions: PPn = (K·τ·f)/(μ·L²) falls from 0.85 (young) to 0.32 (old) using f = 1 Hz, μ = 0.7 Pa·s, L = 150 µm.
Restoring K via osmotic agents raises PPn by 0.2 and improves clearance by 18 %.
PPn correlates with DTI‑ALPS index (R² = 0.81).
key_assumptions: Poroelastic pump theory applies at the perivascular scale.
Other transport mechanisms (e.g., ISMT) are secondary.
